The Republic of the Union of Myanmar was a quasi-civilian parliamentary republic in Myanmar from 2008 to 2021. The state was established to replace the military junta, known as the State Peace and Development Council (SPDC), which had ruled the country since 1988. The transition was initiated following the 2010 general elections and the implementation of the 2008 Constitution, drafted by the military. However, on 1 February 2021, the government was overthrown in a coup d'état led by Min Aung Hlaing, the Commander-in-Chief of the Defense Services (Tatmadaw). This marked the end of the 2011–2021 democratic transition and led to the reinstatement of full military rule under the State Administration Council (SAC). While many international bodies and the National Unity Government (NUG) claim continuity of the democratic administration, the republican institutions effectively ceased to function on the mainland following the coup.
History
On 9 April 2008, the Junta adopted a constitution that got ratified on 29 May 2008, and came into effect on 31 January 2011. In March 2011, the military junta was officially dissolved, and Thein Sein, a former general, was inaugurated as the first civilian president in decades. His administration launched a series of landmark political and economic reforms, including the legalization of trade unions, the easing of media censorship, and the release of hundreds of political prisoners. A key turning point occurred in 2012 when the opposition leader and Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi was elected to Parliament in by-elections, signaling the end of her long-standing house arrest and the reintegration of the National League for Democracy (NLD) into the formal political process.
In November 2015, the NLD won a landslide victory in the general elections, marking the first time power was transferred from a military-backed government to a civilian-led one. Since the constitution barred her from the presidency, Aung San Suu Kyi assumed the newly created role of State Counsellor, acting as the de facto head of government. Despite this shift, the Tatmadaw retained significant power under the 2008 Constitution, which guaranteed the military 25% of all parliamentary seats and control over the ministries of Defense, Home Affairs, and Border Affairs.
Conflict and Human Rights
The period was characterized by continued internal conflict between the central government and various Ethnic Armed Organizations (EAOs). Most notably, in 2017, a series of attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) triggered a massive military "clearance operation" in Rakhine State. This led to the displacement of over 700,000 Rohingya Muslims to neighboring Bangladesh. The United Nations and several international organizations labeled the crackdown as "ethnic cleansing" and "genocide," severely damaging the international reputation of the NLD government and Aung San Suu Kyi, who defended the military's actions at the International Court of Justice.
Collapse
Following the November 2020 general elections, in which the NLD won another overwhelming majority, the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and the Tatmadaw alleged widespread voter fraud. Despite the Union Election Commission's dismissal of these claims, the military seized power in the early hours of 1 February 2021.
President Win Myint, State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi, and other senior NLD members were detained. The military declared a one-year state of emergency and transferred all executive, legislative, and judicial powers to Min Aung Hlaing. The institutions of the republic collapsed as the Tatmadaw moved to crush the subsequent Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM). This led to the formation of the People's Defense Forces (PDF) and the escalation of the crisis into a nationwide armed conflict, effectively ending the decade of democratic reform.
